prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its translation into long-acting incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: All six of us ranked GLP-1 first, and I do not treat that as proof of merit, so I restate the scientific case. The arc runs from incretin physiology and proglucagon processing, through the demonstration of GLP-1 action in humans and its intestinotropic and metabolic biology, to acylated long-acting analogues that now have large independent outcome trials in type 2 diabetes, obesity, cardiovascular and renal disease. The mechanism is stable, the replication is extensive, and the patient impact is unusually large and still widening. The prize configuration I prefer pairs two people who defined the hormone's physiology and biology (Holst, Drucker) with the person who led the pharmacological design that made it a medicine (Knudsen), so the citation covers both discovery and translation.
statement.case_against: The credit problem is real and cannot be resolved by the three-person limit. Mojsov's identification and synthesis of the active truncated peptide, and the early work of Habener and colleagues on proglucagon-derived peptides, are arguably as foundational as some of what the preferred trio is credited for, and priority disputes there are not settled by the evidence in front of us. Including Knudsen also makes a judgement that industrial drug design is part of the discovery, which some colleagues may reject. The other reservation is that a prize this obviously deserved can stay unresolved only because of attribution, and I would not want the committee to settle that by default, from familiarity or from the unanimity of opening ballots.

responses.point: Svenningsson proposed Drucker, Holst and Mojsov for B014, treating Mojsov's identification of the active peptide as part of the discovery core, while calling Knudsen a strong candidate who is left out.
responses.response: I take Mojsov's claim seriously, and it is the main point on which I am unsure of my own configuration. Identifying and synthesising the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide was an enabling step for the insulinotropic work. My hesitation is that a prize without Knudsen leaves out the step that turned the biology into liraglutide and semaglutide, which is the main reason this topic is now on the table in 2026. Between the two, I weigh the physiological and pharmacological chain as a whole. If the committee sees the prize as recognising a discovery, your trio is defensible. If it recognises the discovery together with its realisation as medicine, I prefer mine. I would like the citation wording to decide this rather than seniority or priority claims.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius argued for a Drucker, Holst and Mojsov configuration, calling Knudsen's medicinal chemistry major but arguably drug development. She also ranked cGAS-STING fourth, with Chen and Barber, as a clear mechanistic discovery relevant to autoimmunity.
responses.response: I partly disagree on the drug-development point. Long-acting acylation to bind albumin was a design insight, not routine optimisation, and our field has recognised design-led translation when it created a new modality. On cGAS-STING I agree the mechanism is strong, and a Chen and Barber pair is cleaner than my own opening, which was cautious about the other credited names. But I would not put it above B014 or B006, because the therapeutic translation is still unproven. A prize here would rest on mechanism alone, which is acceptable, but I would want to see more than early-stage agonists and antagonists before preferring it to a modality already helping many patients.

responses.point: El-Manira ranked optogenetics second, proposing Deisseroth, Hegemann and Nagel, and he accepted that this three-person limit forces the exclusion of Bamberg, Boyden and Miesenböck.
responses.response: I agree the science of B008 is mature and has changed experimental neuroscience, and I have it in my top four. My reservation is the attribution problem you describe, which is more severe than for B014. At least six credited people have defensible claims and any trio excludes someone central, especially Bamberg's early channelrhodopsin electrophysiology or Boyden's parallel neuronal work. Also, the main impact is as a research tool, with clinical use only beginning, so it competes less well with B014 or B006. I would keep it as a strong alternative, and would revisit it if the committee wants a basic-science part alongside a therapeutic one.

uncertainties: Whether the prize should credit Mojsov for the active peptide, Knudsen for the long-acting analogues, or both, and how the three-person limit should be used.
Whether the committee treats pharmaceutical design as a discovery in its own right or as development to be left outside the citation.
Whether pairing B014 with a second achievement such as CAR-T is better than a single-topic prize, given that the name limit would then force awkward cuts in the credited names.
I cannot verify the latest long-term safety and outcome data on incretin therapies from the supplied materials.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B014, B006, B008 or the other shortlisted candidates. I have co-authored with Sten Linnarsson and Jonas Frisén on single-cell work, but none of the shortlisted ballots concerns that work or those people. Shared KI affiliation is not itself a connection to any credited candidate.
